> 名與身孰親？身與貨孰多？得與亡孰病？

Chapter 43 was about the outside: why the soft can run through the hard. Chapter 44 turns inward, all the way in, to a single question: what do you actually want?

Three questions, each closer than the last.

Is name or body closer to you? Is body or goods heavier? Is gaining or losing the greater illness?

Then a verdict: 甚愛必大費，多藏必厚亡. Then a way out: 知足不辱，知止不殆.

And the four characters most often read past are the way out.

## 足 is a foot, 止 is a toe

This is not a rhetorical detail — it is the whole chapter.

足 is the foot. 知足 is knowing where your foot is standing: what ground you are actually on, how much weight it can hold.

止 is the toe, the stopping of the foot. 知止 is knowing where the foot should stop — not "don't be greedy," but knowing the precise point at which stepping forward would put you off the ground you are on.

Laozi is not giving a mood instruction. He is describing a person who has a sense of position and a sense of limit, the way a body has a sense of balance.

Which is why the results are physical too: 不辱 — not disgraced, because you never claimed a ground you weren't standing on. 不殆 — not imperiled, because you never walked past the edge.

## 名與身孰親

名 can reach you and body cannot be reached by it. A name travels anywhere; a body is here, and has a location, a weight, a limit.

孰親 asks which is closer — and the answer is already in the structure: one of them is where you live, the other is a label applied from outside.

## 身與貨孰多

多 here is not quantity; it is 分量 — weight, how much a thing weighs in the scale of a life.

So the question is not "do you have too much stuff" but: which of these two carries more weight in your decisions? The body is what carries; goods are what is carried.

## 得與亡孰病

病 is the specific word for illness — a malfunction, not misfortune.

Which is the sickness: gaining, or losing? The question reverses the obvious answer. Losing is an event; the craving to gain is a condition. One happens to you; the other runs inside you continuously.

## 甚愛必大費，多藏必厚亡

Love something excessively, and the expenditure will be great. Store much, and the loss will be thick.

Both sentences describe the same arithmetic: what is held at high value requires high maintenance, and the maintenance is drawn from the same account as the life.

厚亡 — thick loss. Not just a large loss, but a loss with the same thickness as the hoard. What you piled up decides the size of the hole when it goes.

## Why this chapter follows 43

43 said: non-forcing works because it leaves no edge to be resisted. 44 asks the prior question — what is it that keeps producing edges?

The answer: valuation. Every 甚愛 is the installation of an edge, and the edge has to be defended, and the defense is the 大費.

知足 and 知止 are the point where the installation stops.

## A test

Name the three things you have most 甚愛'd in the past year. Then count the hours spent maintaining them. The ratio is the chapter's argument, in your own numbers.
